opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by stepping back from the robot entirely and asking what the person actually needs done. A lot of the time the honest answer is that a humanoid isn't the right tool. If the task is repetitive, happens in a fixed location, and the environment can be engineered around it, then a robot arm, a conveyor, or a specialized machine will almost always be cheaper, faster, and more reliable. Humanoids are a very general and very expensive solution, so you should only reach for them when generality is really what's needed.

So the first filter is the environment. Was the space built for humans, and does it need to stay that way? Homes, hospitals, older factories, warehouses with stairs and narrow aisles, places full of door handles, shelves, and tools sized for human hands. If you can't or won't redesign that space, then a human-shaped body starts to make sense, because it can move through the same world and use the same objects without you rebuilding everything.

The second filter is task diversity. If the user needs one thing done ten thousand times, specialize. If they need fifty different things done a few times each, like loading a dishwasher, then folding laundry, then carrying a box upstairs, that's where a general-purpose embodiment pays off. The value of a humanoid comes from amortizing one platform across many tasks.

Third, I look at tolerance for failure and safety. Humanoids today are still not as reliable as people would like. So I ask what happens when it drops something, misjudges a grasp, or loses balance. If a mistake is cheap and recoverable, you can deploy earlier and learn from real data. If a mistake could hurt someone, like in eldercare, the bar is much higher, and you might want a more constrained form factor first.

And finally, there's the human side. Sometimes people are more comfortable working alongside something whose motions they can read and predict, and a humanoid form helps with that. But sometimes it raises expectations the robot can't meet. If it looks like a person, people expect it to understand like a person. So part of judging the fit is being honest with the user about what the system can and can't do today.

So in short: unstructured human environment, high task variety, manageable failure costs, and a user who understands the current limits. When those line up, a humanoid is a good fit. When they don't, I'd rather recommend something simpler that actually solves the problem.

r002.rationale: It says to start by asking what the person needs done and notes that a humanoid often is not the right tool.

r003.rationale: It recommends specialized machines for repetitive tasks and simpler tools when a humanoid’s generality is unnecessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I start by being suspicious of the humanoid form itself. The question I ask first is not "can a humanoid do this?" but "why does this task need a body shaped like a person at all?" If the honest answer is that it doesn't, then a humanoid is probably the wrong tool, and you should look at a wheeled base with an arm, a fixed manipulator, or no robot at all.

Where the humanoid earns its place is when the environment was built for humans and you cannot change it. Stairs, narrow doorways, shelves at chest height, tools with handles designed for a hand. If the user is a hospital or a home or an older factory, retrofitting the space is often more expensive than adapting the robot. That's when the form factor stops being a gimmick and becomes a real constraint-matching decision.

The second thing I look at is task variety. A humanoid is a generalist, and generalists are expensive and slower than specialists. If the user has one repetitive task, I'd tell them to buy the specialized machine. If they have fifty different small tasks across a day, and those tasks keep changing, that's where the flexibility pays off.

Then there's the uncomfortable part, which is reliability and safety. I ask what happens when the robot fails. If a failure means a dropped box, fine. If it means a fall next to a patient, the bar is completely different, and most humanoids today don't clear it. So part of judging fit is being honest about the maturity of the technology, not just the demo video.

And finally I talk to the actual users, not the person signing the purchase order. A robot that the night-shift staff find creepy or annoying will get unplugged within a month. So I'd say the right tool is the one that matches the space, matches the task mix, survives its own failures, and that the people around it actually want to work with.

r002.rationale: It says to ask why the task needs a humanoid and recommends other tools when they better fit the user's need.

r003.rationale: It says humanoids are expensive generalists and recommends a specialized machine for a single repetitive task.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the user’s problem, not with the robot. What task do they need done, in what environment, and what does success look like? Then I’d ask whether a simpler tool could do it better. If a fixed robot arm or a wheeled robot can solve the problem reliably at a lower cost, that may be the right answer.

A humanoid becomes interesting when the environment is designed for people and the work requires moving between different tasks—using existing tools, reaching different heights, navigating spaces that are difficult to modify. But looking human isn’t itself a benefit. You have to connect that form to something the user actually needs.

Ultimately, I’d judge it by performance in the real workflow: Can it complete the task safely and reliably? How much human intervention does it need? And does the value it creates justify the total cost? A compelling demonstration is a starting point; the useful test is whether it makes the user’s day better.

r002.rationale: It says to start with the user’s problem rather than the robot and asks whether a simpler tool could solve it better.

r003.rationale: It explains that a fixed arm or wheeled robot may be the better choice when it can solve the task reliably at lower cost, while describing when a humanoid’s ability to handle varied tasks is useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start with the user’s problem, rather than the robot’s form. What task do they need done, in what environment, and what would count as success? Then I’d ask whether a humanoid is actually the simplest way to deliver that outcome. Could a fixed arm, a wheeled robot, or a change to the workflow do it more reliably and at lower cost?

The case for a humanoid becomes stronger when the environment is designed for people and you need to perform several different tasks without rebuilding that environment. But looking human isn’t enough. You still have to show that it can do the work safely, reliably, and at a cost the user can justify—including maintenance and the times a person has to step in.

So my test would be: does having a human-shaped body solve a real constraint for this user? If it does, great. If it doesn’t, we should be willing to choose a different tool.

r001.rationale: The response mentions alternative robot forms, but says nothing about delivering the same image-capture experience.

r002.rationale: It says to start with the user’s problem and ask whether a humanoid is the simplest way to achieve the outcome.

r003.rationale: It explains that a fixed arm or wheeled robot may be simpler and more reliable, and that a humanoid’s broad task range does not make it the right choice for every scenario.
